text: Anemia: Anemia is a blood disorder in which the blood has a reduced ability to carry oxygen. This can be due to a lower than normal number of red blood cells, a reduction in the amount of hemoglobin available for oxygen transport, or abnormalities in hemoglobin that impair its function.

Bleeding: Bleeding, hemorrhage, haemorrhage or blood loss, is blood escaping from the circulatory system from damaged blood vessels. Bleeding can occur internally, or externally either through a natural opening such as the mouth, nose, ear, urethra, genitalia or anus, or through a puncture in the skin.
Hypovolemia is a massive decrease in blood volume, and death by excessive loss of blood is referred to as exsanguination.

Lymphadenopathy: Lymphadenopathy or adenopathy is a disease of the lymph nodes, in which they are abnormal in size or consistency. Lymphadenopathy of an inflammatory type is lymphadenitis, producing swollen or enlarged lymph nodes.

Polycythemia: Polycythemia is a medical condition suggested by a laboratory finding that the hematocrit and/or hemoglobin concentration are increased in the blood, although this finding is also present in capillary leak syndrome. Polycythemia is sometimes called erythrocytosis, and there is significant overlap in the two findings, but the terms are not the same: polycythemia describes any increase in hematocrit and/or hemoglobin, while erythrocytosis describes an increase specifically in the number of red blood cells in the blood.
Recurrent infections: A presenting complaint characterised by recurrent infections.
Splenomegaly: Splenomegaly is an enlargement of the spleen. The spleen usually lies in the left upper quadrant (LUQ) of the human abdomen.

Thrombosis: Thrombosis is the formation of a blood clot inside a blood vessel, obstructing the flow of blood through the circulatory system. When a blood vessel is injured, the body uses platelets (thrombocytes) and fibrin to form a blood clot to prevent blood loss.

Risk factors: Blood Loss, Decreased Red Blood Cell Production, Increased Red Blood Cell Breakdown. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Anemia, unspecified red flags. Red flag (RF_ANEMIA) triggered by complaint 'ANEMIA': [LLM DRAFT] Severe symptomatic anemia with hemodynamic instability, chest pain, or acute shortness of breath at rest.. Red flag (RF_BLEEDING) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Active, uncontrolled hemorrhage or severe bleeding manifestations such as purpura fulminans or gastrointestinal bleeding leading to hemodynamic compromise..

Anemia, unspecified differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Aplastic Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Pancytopenia with a markedly hypocellular bone marrow Compared to Nutritional Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Specific dietary deficiencies or macro/microcytic indices responding to targeted supplementation Compared to Refractory Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Persistent anemia unresponsive to standard hematinic therapy requiring bone marrow evaluation

Aplastic anemia, unspecified: Aplastic anemia (AA) is a severe hematologic condition in which the body fails to make blood cells in sufficient numbers. Normally, blood cells are produced in the bone marrow by stem cells that reside there, but patients with aplastic anemia have a deficiency of all blood cell types: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Common presenting complaints: Anemia, Recurrent Infections. Associated symptoms: Pale Skin, Fatigue, Fast Heart Rate, Rash, Dizziness, Headache, Frequent Or Prolonged Infections, Nosebleeds, Bleeding Gums, Prolonged Bleeding From Cuts, Unexplained Or Easy Bruising, Hematoma. Risk factors: Smoking, Ionizing Radiation, Some Chemicals, Prior Chemotherapy, Down Syndrome. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Aplastic anemia, unspecified red flags. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_THROMBOCYTOPENIA_LEADING_TO_LIFE_THREATENING_HEMORRHAGE) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Spontaneous or uncontrolled bleeding such as intracranial hemorrhage, severe epistaxis, or massive gastrointestinal bleeding. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_NEUTROPENIA_COMPLICATED_BY_OVERWHELMING_SEPSIS) triggered by complaint 'RECURRENT_INFECTIONS': [LLM DRAFT] High fever, rigors, and signs of septic shock in a profoundly immunocompromised patient.

Aplastic anemia, unspecified differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Idiopathic Aplastic Anemia: [LLM DRAFT] Confirmed absence of secondary causes such as toxins, drugs, or viral infections. Compared to Fanconi Anemia: [LLM DRAFT] Presence of congenital physical anomalies and genetic mutation testing. Compared to Refractory Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Bone marrow typically shows cellular dysplasia rather than profound hypocellularity.

Chronic congestive splenomegaly red flags. Red flag (RF_BLEEDING_CRISIS) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Acute, severe hemorrhage resulting from portal hypertension-induced variceal rupture or severe thrombocytopenia associated with hypersplenism.. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_THROMBOTIC_EVENT) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] Acute portal vein thrombosis or splenic vein thrombosis causing sudden worsening of abdominal pain and congestion..

Chronic congestive splenomegaly differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Neutropenic Splenomegaly: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with prominent neutropenia and recurrent infections rather than primarily portal hypertension and congestion. Compared to Portal Vein Thrombosis: [LLM DRAFT] Directly causes presinusoidal portal hypertension and congestive splenomegaly via acute or chronic occlusion of the main portal vein. Compared to Esophageal Varices With Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Represents a severe, acute hemorrhagic complication driven by the elevated portal pressures underlying chronic congestive splenomegaly.

Duodenitis with bleeding: Duodenitis is inflammation of the duodenum. It may persist acutely or chronically. Common presenting complaints: Bleeding. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Duodenitis with bleeding red flags. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_GI_HEMORRHAGE) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Active, profuse gastrointestinal bleeding manifested by hematemesis, melena, or hemodynamic instability resulting from the duodenitis.. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_SYMPTOMATIC_ANEMIA) triggered by complaint 'ANEMIA': [LLM DRAFT] Critical drop in hemoglobin secondary to chronic or acute duodenal bleeding, presenting with acute shortness of breath, chest pain, syncope, or severe dizziness..

Duodenitis with bleeding differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Duodenitis Without Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Confirmed presence of mucosal inflammation without active hemorrhage or blood loss on endoscopy. Compared to Esophageal Varices With Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Hematemesis often associated with portal hypertension and stigmata of chronic liver disease rather than proximal small bowel inflammation. Compared to Other Esophagitis With Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Upper gastrointestinal bleeding originating from the distal esophagus rather than the duodenal bulb, typically presenting with retrosternal discomfort or heartburn.

Duodenitis without bleeding: Duodenitis is inflammation of the duodenum. It may persist acutely or chronically. Common presenting complaints: Bleeding. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Duodenitis without bleeding red flags. Red flag (RF_BLEEDING) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Development of active gastrointestinal bleeding manifesting as hematemesis, melena, or significant hemoglobin drop despite prior non-bleeding classification..

Duodenitis without bleeding differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Duodenitis With Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with overt gastrointestinal bleeding such as melena or hematemesis rather than just non-bleeding dyspeptic symptoms. Compared to Esophageal Varices Without Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Associated with portal hypertension and distinct endoscopic findings in the esophagus rather than the duodenum. Compared to Other Esophagitis Without Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Inflammation located in the esophagus typically causing retrosternal chest pain or heartburn instead of duodenal discomfort.

Embolism and thrombosis of iliac artery: A sudden or progressive blockage of the iliac artery due to a blood clot or embolus, leading to ischemia of the lower extremities. Common presenting complaints: Thrombosis. Associated symptoms: Pain, Swelling, Redness, Enlarged Veins In The Affected Limb. Risk factors: Recent Surgery, Older Age, Active Cancer, Obesity, Infection, Smoking, Inflammatory Diseases, Antiphospholipid Syndrome, Personal History Or Family History Of Vte, Injuries, Trauma, Lack Of Movement. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Embolism and thrombosis of iliac artery red flags. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_LIMB_ISCHEMIA) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] Sudden onset of severe pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, and paralysis in the affected lower extremity due to acute iliac artery occlusion..

Embolism and thrombosis of iliac artery differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Embolism And Thrombosis Of Other Arteries: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with acute ischemia affecting a different arterial bed, such as the upper extremities or visceral vessels, rather than the lower limb and pelvic ischemia typical of iliac occlusion. Compared to Embolism And Thrombosis Of Thoracic Aorta: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with signs of proximal major trunk obstruction, such as acute upper and lower extremity perfusion deficits or back pain, rather than isolated unilateral lower extremity ischemia. Compared to Embolism And Thrombosis Of Unspecified Artery: [LLM DRAFT] Represents an unlocalized vascular occlusion lacking the specific anatomic localization to the iliac bifurcation that characterizes lower limb claudication, rest pain, or pulselessness.

Embolism and thrombosis of other arteries: A hematology condition known as Embolism and thrombosis of other arteries. Common presenting complaints: Thrombosis. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Embolism and thrombosis of other arteries red flags. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_ARTERIAL_OCCLUSION) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] Sudden onset of severe pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, and paralysis in an affected limb indicating acute peripheral arterial ischemia..

Embolism and thrombosis of other arteries differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Embolism And Thrombosis Of Iliac Artery: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with acute lower limb ischemia, rest pain, or absent femoral/popliteal pulses rather than ischemia localized to visceral or upper extremity vascular beds. Compared to Embolism And Thrombosis Of Thoracic Aorta: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with symptoms of acute aortic syndrome, such as tearing chest or back pain and upper-to-lower body blood pressure differentials, rather than peripheral or visceral arterial occlusion. Compared to Embolism And Thrombosis Of Unspecified Artery: [LLM DRAFT] Represents an unspecified vascular site requiring further anatomical imaging to localize the occlusion compared to clearly specified arterial beds.

Embolism and thrombosis of thoracic aorta: A hematology condition known as Embolism and thrombosis of thoracic aorta. Common presenting complaints: Thrombosis. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Embolism and thrombosis of thoracic aorta red flags. Red flag (RF_AORTIC_THROMBOSIS_CAUSING_ACUTE_LIMB_ISCHEMIA_OR_VISCERALRENAL_INFARCTION) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] When acute thrombosis of the thoracic aorta leads to sudden, severe limb ischemia (pain, pallor, pulselessness) or end-organ ischemia..

Embolism and thrombosis of thoracic aorta differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Embolism And Thrombosis Of Iliac Artery: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with lower extremity ischemia and absent femoral or distal pulses rather than chest or back pain. Compared to Embolism And Thrombosis Of Unspecified Artery: [LLM DRAFT] Lacks anatomical localization to the thoracic aorta and requires imaging to identify the specific site of occlusion. Compared to Intracardiac Thrombosis Not Elsewhere Classified: [LLM DRAFT] Involves thrombus formation within cardiac chambers rather than the great vessels of the thorax.

Embolism and thrombosis of unspecified artery: Sudden blockage of an unspecified artery by an embolus or thrombus, causing ischemia of downstream tissues. Common presenting complaints: Thrombosis. Associated symptoms: Shortness Of Breath, Chest Pain, Coughing Up Blood. Risk factors: Cancer, Prolonged Bed Rest, Blunt Trauma, Smoking, Stroke, Certain Genetic Conditions, Estrogen Based Medication, Pregnancy, Obesity, After Surgery. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Embolism and thrombosis of unspecified artery red flags. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_ARTERIAL_OCCLUSION) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] Sudden onset of severe pain, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paresthesia, or paralysis in an affected limb indicating critical ischemia.. Red flag (RF_HEMORRHAGIC_TRANSFORMATION_OR_RUPTURE) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Active, uncontrolled hemorrhage or signs of internal bleeding secondary to vascular occlusion or anticoagulant therapy..

Embolism and thrombosis of unspecified artery differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Embolism And Thrombosis Of Iliac Artery: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with acute lower extremity ischemia, claudication, or absent distal pulses localized specifically to the lower limbs. Compared to Embolism And Thrombosis Of Thoracic Aorta: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with acute chest or back pain, upper-to-lower extremity blood pressure discrepancies, or symptoms of aortic arch syndrome. Compared to Embolism And Thrombosis Of Other Arteries: [LLM DRAFT] Involves specifically identified visceral, upper extremity, or carotid arterial beds rather than an unspecified anatomical location.

Esophageal varices with bleeding: Esophageal varices are extremely dilated sub-mucosal veins in the lower third of the esophagus. They are most often a consequence of portal hypertension, commonly due to cirrhosis. Common presenting complaints: Bleeding. Associated symptoms: Vomiting Blood, Passing Black Stool. Risk factors: Or Liver Based, Circulation). Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Esophageal varices with bleeding red flags. Red flag (RF_MASSIVE_GASTROINTESTINAL_HEMORRHAGE) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Active, profuse hematemesis or melena accompanied by hemodynamic instability, hypotension, or altered mental status indicating acute massive blood loss from esophageal varices.. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_ACUTE_ANEMIA_FROM_VARICEAL_BLEED) triggered by complaint 'ANEMIA': [LLM DRAFT] Rapidly developing profound anemia due to acute variceal bleeding resulting in symptomatic tachycardia, dizziness, or syncope..

Esophageal varices with bleeding differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Esophageal Varices Without Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with similar portal hypertension risks and venous dilation on endoscopy, but lacks acute hemorrhage. Compared to Duodenitis With Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with upper gastrointestinal bleeding originating from the proximal small bowel rather than dilated submucosal esophageal veins. Compared to Other Esophagitis With Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to mucosal inflammation and ulceration rather than ruptured portal-systemic collaterals.

Esophageal varices without bleeding: Esophageal varices are extremely dilated sub-mucosal veins in the lower third of the esophagus. Esophageal varices without bleeding red flags. Red flag (RF_BLEEDING) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Acute gastrointestinal bleeding manifested as hematemesis or melena due to variceal rupture..

Esophageal varices without bleeding differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Esophageal Varices With Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with hematemesis or melena rather than being incidentally found or asymptomatic. Compared to Other Esophagitis Without Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with retrosternal chest pain or heartburn rather than submucosal venous dilation. Compared to Duodenitis Without Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with epigastric pain and duodenal mucosal inflammation rather than lower esophageal venous varices.

Familial erythrocytosis: Polycythemia is a medical condition suggested by a laboratory finding that the hematocrit and/or hemoglobin concentration are increased in the blood, although this finding is also present in capillary leak syndrome. Polycythemia is sometimes called erythrocytosis, and there is significant overlap in the two findings, but the terms are not the same: polycythemia describes any increase in hematocrit and/or hemoglobin, while erythrocytosis describes an increase specifically in the number of red blood cells in the blood. Common presenting complaints: Polycythemia. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Familial erythrocytosis red flags. Red flag (RF_THROMBOSIS) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] Acute arterial or venous thromboembolism due to severe erythrocytosis-induced hyperviscosity..

Familial erythrocytosis differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Polycythemia Vera: [LLM DRAFT] Often presents with panmyelosis, splenomegaly, and JAK2 mutations rather than isolated erythrocytosis. Compared to Secondary Polycythemia: [LLM DRAFT] Usually caused by chronic hypoxia, high-altitude exposure, or erythropoietin-secreting tumors with elevated serum EPO levels. Compared to Neonatal Jaundice Due To Polycythemia: [LLM DRAFT] Manifests strictly in newborns with hyperbilirubinemia secondary to an elevated hematocrit.

Fanconi anemia: Fanconi anemia (FA), also known as Fanconi cancer, is a rare, autosomal recessive genetic disease characterized by aplastic anemia, congenital defects, endocrinological abnormalities, and an increased incidence of developing cancer. The study of Fanconi anemia has improved scientific understanding of the mechanisms of normal bone marrow function and the development of cancer. Common presenting complaints: Anemia, Recurrent Infections. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Fanconi anemia red flags. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_BONE_MARROW_FAILURE_AND_THROMBOCYTOPENIA) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Spontaneous or uncontrolled major bleeding (e.g., epistaxis, petechiae, GI bleeding) due to severe thrombocytopenia. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_NEUTROPENIA_WITH_SEPSIS) triggered by complaint 'RECURRENT_INFECTIONS': [LLM DRAFT] High fever and signs of severe infection in a patient with bone marrow failure.

Fanconi anemia differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Aplastic Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with bone marrow failure similar to Fanconi anemia, but lacks the characteristic congenital physical malformations and chromosomal fragility testing abnormalities. Compared to Idiopathic Aplastic Anemia: [LLM DRAFT] Acquired form of marrow failure that typically occurs in older children or adults without the inherited genetic mutations or characteristic somatic stigmata (e.g., thumb/radial defects) seen in Fanconi anemia. Compared to Refractory Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Features persistent cytopenias resembling early Fanconi anemia, but generally lacks the multi-system congenital anomalies and DNA cross-linking agent hypersensitivity definitive of the disorder.

Idiopathic aplastic anemia: A hematology condition known as Idiopathic aplastic anemia. Common presenting complaints: Anemia, Recurrent Infections. Associated symptoms: Pale Skin, Fatigue, Fast Heart Rate, Rash, Dizziness, Headache, Frequent Or Prolonged Infections, Nosebleeds, Bleeding Gums, Prolonged Bleeding From Cuts, Unexplained Or Easy Bruising, Hematoma. Risk factors: Smoking, Ionizing Radiation, Some Chemicals, Prior Chemotherapy, Down Syndrome. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Idiopathic aplastic anemia red flags. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_BLEEDING_MANIFESTATIONS) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Spontaneous mucosal bleeding, severe epistaxis, or signs of intracranial hemorrhage due to profound thrombocytopenia.. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_NEUTROPENIC_FEVER) triggered by complaint 'RECURRENT_INFECTIONS': [LLM DRAFT] Fever of 38.3°C or higher (or 38.0°C sustained for over an hour) in the setting of severe neutropenia indicating life-threatening infection..

Idiopathic aplastic anemia differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Fanconi Anemia: [LLM DRAFT] Presence of congenital physical anomalies such as thumb or radial ray defects and shorter stature. Compared to Aplastic Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Lack of a confirmed negative workup for secondary causes such as drugs, toxins, or viral infections. Compared to Refractory Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Typically exhibits bone marrow dysplasia rather than purely hypocellular marrow with normal cytogenetics.

Intracardiac thrombosis, not elsewhere classified: A hematology condition known as Intracardiac thrombosis, not elsewhere classified. Common presenting complaints: Thrombosis. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Intracardiac thrombosis, not elsewhere classified red flags. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_LIMB_ISCHEMIA_OR_DEEP_VEIN_THROMBOSIS) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] Acute onset of severe pain, pallor, pulselessness, or swelling in an extremity indicating thromboembolic occlusion secondary to intracardiac thrombus.. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_ACUTE_GASTROINTESTINAL_OR_MUCOSAL_HEMORRHAGE) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Sudden, profuse bleeding or hemorrhagic manifestations associated with consumptive coagulopathy or anticoagulant therapy complications related to intracardiac thrombosis..

Intracardiac thrombosis, not elsewhere classified differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Embolism And Thrombosis Of Thoracic Aorta: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with signs of distal malperfusion, back pain, or pulse deficits rather than primary cardiac chamber filling defects or valvular/ventricular dysfunction. Compared to Nonpyogenic Thrombosis Of Intracranial Venous System: [LLM DRAFT] Manifests primarily with neurological symptoms such as headache, seizures, or focal deficits due to cerebral venous outflow obstruction. Compared to Portal Vein Thrombosis: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by abdominal pain, portal hypertension, or gastrointestinal bleeding rather than intracardiac embolic events.

Neonatal jaundice due to polycythemia: Neonatal jaundice, clinically known as neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and icterus neonatorum, is the yellowish discoloration of the white part of the eyes (sclerae) and skin in newborn infants caused by an elevated concentration of bilirubin in the blood (hyperbilirubinemia). It is one of the most frequently encountered medical conditions in the neonatal period, affecting approximately 60% of term and 80% preterm newborns within the first week of life. Common presenting complaints: Polycythemia. Associated symptoms: Yellowish Coloration Of Skin And Sclera, Itchiness. Risk factors: High Bilirubin Levels. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Neonatal jaundice due to polycythemia red flags. Red flag (RF_THROMBOSIS_PRESENTATION) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] Marked hyperviscosity leading to acute vessel occlusion, stroke, or deep vein thrombosis in a neonate with polycythemia-induced jaundice. Red flag (RF_BLEEDING_DIATHESIS) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Active hemorrhage or disseminated intravascular coagulation secondary to severe neonatal polycythemia and hyperviscosity.

Neonatal jaundice due to polycythemia differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Polycythemia Neonatorum: [LLM DRAFT] Elevated central hematocrit without necessarily presenting with clinically significant unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Compared to Secondary Polycythemia: [LLM DRAFT] Presents in older patients often in response to chronic hypoxia rather than as a newborn hematologic adaptation. Compared to Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with pallor and low hemoglobin rather than a ruddy complexion and high hematocrit.

Neutropenic splenomegaly: A hematology condition known as Neutropenic splenomegaly. Common presenting complaints: Splenomegaly, Recurrent Infections. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: Infections, Malignancies, Non Infectious Inflammatory Diseases, Others. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Neutropenic splenomegaly red flags. Red flag (RF_SPLENIC_RUPTURE_WITH_MASSIVE_INTERNAL_HEMORRHAGE) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Sudden severe left upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the left shoulder (Kehr's sign) accompanied by acute hemodynamic instability, dizziness, or signs of hemorrhagic shock in a patient with neutropenic splenomegaly.. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_OVERWHELMING_SEPSIS) triggered by complaint 'RECURRENT_INFECTIONS': [LLM DRAFT] High fever, rigors, altered mental status, and profound hypotension in a severely neutropenic patient with an enlarged spleen, indicating potential septic shock..

Neutropenic splenomegaly differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Chronic Congestive Splenomegaly: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with signs of portal hypertension rather than primary neutropenia-associated infections. Compared to Aplastic Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by pancytopenia with a hypocellular bone marrow rather than isolated or primary neutropenia with splenic enlargement. Compared to Portal Vein Thrombosis: [LLM DRAFT] Marked by abdominal pain and imaging evidence of venous obstruction rather than immune-mediated or hypersplenism-driven neutropenia.

Nonpyogenic thrombosis of intracranial venous system: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST), cerebral venous and sinus thrombosis or cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT), is the presence of a blood clot in the dural venous sinuses, the cerebral veins, or both. Symptoms may include severe headache, visual symptoms, any of the symptoms of stroke such as weakness of the face and limbs on one side of the body, and seizures, which occur in around 40% of patients. Common presenting complaints: Thrombosis. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Nonpyogenic thrombosis of intracranial venous system red flags. Red flag (RF_THROMBOSIS) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] Acute intracranial hypertension or cerebral edema resulting in papilledema, rapidly progressive focal neurological deficits, or depressed mental status secondary to extensive venous sinus occlusion.. Red flag (RF_BLEEDING) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Acute hemorrhagic venous infarction manifesting as sudden severe headache, focal seizures, or acute neurological deterioration..

Nonpyogenic thrombosis of intracranial venous system differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Portal Vein Thrombosis: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with signs of portal hypertension and abdominal pain rather than isolated intracranial hypertension and neurological deficits. Compared to Polycythemia Vera: [LLM DRAFT] Associated with generalized erythrocytosis, splenomegaly, and hyperviscosity symptoms instead of localized cerebral venous outflow obstruction. Compared to Intracardiac Thrombosis Not Elsewhere Classified: [LLM DRAFT] Manifests primarily with cardiac dysfunction or systemic arterial embolization rather than localized cerebral venous sinus occlusion.

Nutritional anemia, unspecified: Anemia is a deficiency in the size or number of red blood cells or in the amount of hemoglobin they contain. This deficiency limits the exchange of O2 and CO2 between the blood and the tissue cells. Common presenting complaints: Anemia. Associated symptoms: Feeling Tired, Shortness Of Breath, Pale Skin, Lightheadedness, Fast Heart Rate, Chest Pain, Burning Or Numbness, And Depression. Risk factors: Nutritional Disorder. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Nutritional anemia, unspecified red flags. Red flag (RF_ANEMIA) triggered by complaint 'ANEMIA': [LLM DRAFT] Severe symptomatic anemia resulting in hemodynamic instability (e.g., resting tachycardia, hypotension, dizziness, or shortness of breath at rest). Red flag (RF_BLEEDING) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Severe or uncontrollable hemorrhage secondary to profound bone marrow suppression or severe thrombocytopenia associated with nutritional deficiency.

Nutritional anemia, unspecified differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Broad classification requiring further laboratory evaluation to confirm a specific nutritional versus non-nutritional etiology. Compared to Aplastic Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with pancytopenia and a hypocellular bone marrow rather than isolated nutritional deficiencies. Compared to Protein Deficiency Anemia: [LLM DRAFT] Specifically linked to inadequate protein intake accompanied by distinctive signs of protein-energy malnutrition.

Other esophagitis with bleeding: Esophagitis, also spelled oesophagitis, is a disease characterized by inflammation of the esophagus. The esophagus is a tube composed of a mucosal lining, and longitudinal and circular smooth muscle fibers. Common presenting complaints: Bleeding. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Other esophagitis with bleeding red flags. Red flag (RF_BLEEDING) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Active, massive hematemesis or melena causing hemodynamic instability, dizziness, or syncope..

Other esophagitis with bleeding differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Esophageal Varices With Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with massive upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage often secondary to portal hypertension rather than mucosal inflammation. Compared to Other Esophagitis Without Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Shares identical inflammatory esophageal symptoms but lacks overt hemorrhage or blood loss. Compared to Duodenitis With Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Causes upper gastrointestinal bleeding originating from the small bowel rather than the esophagus.

Other esophagitis without bleeding: Esophagitis, also spelled oesophagitis, is a disease characterized by inflammation of the esophagus. The esophagus is a tube composed of a mucosal lining, and longitudinal and circular smooth muscle fibers. Common presenting complaints: Bleeding. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Other esophagitis without bleeding differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Other Esophagitis With Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Presence of acute hemorrhage, hematemesis, or melena on presentation rather than purely inflammatory symptoms like dysphagia or heartburn. Compared to Esophageal Varices Without Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Endoscopic visualization of dilated submucosal veins rather than inflammatory mucosal changes or ulcerations. Compared to Duodenitis Without Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Inflammation localized to the duodenal bulb and small intestine rather than the esophageal mucosa, typically presenting with epigastric pain related to meals.

Ovulation bleeding: Ovulation bleeding is a brief, light vaginal discharge that occurs around the time of ovulation, typically lasting a few hours to a day. Common presenting complaints: Bleeding. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Ovulation bleeding red flags. Red flag (RF_OVULATION_BLEEDING_HEAVY_BLEEDING) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Heavy bleeding > 500 mL or continuous > 48 hrs. Red flag (RF_OVULATION_BLEEDING_ANEMIA) triggered by complaint 'ANEMIA': [LLM DRAFT] Severe anemia (Hb < 7 g/dL) or symptomatic anemia with heavy bleeding.

Ovulation bleeding differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Postmenopausal Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Occurs after the cessation of menses rather than mid-cycle in premenopausal individuals Compared to Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with generalized fatigue and low hemoglobin rather than cyclic mid-cycle spotting

Perianal venous thrombosis: A hematology condition known as Perianal venous thrombosis. Common presenting complaints: Thrombosis. Associated symptoms: Abdominal Pain, Diarrhea (may Be Bloody), Fever, Weight Loss. Risk factors: Uncertain. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Perianal venous thrombosis red flags. Red flag (RF_PERIANAL_VENOUS_THROMBOSIS_BLEEDING) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Profuse perianal bleeding with hemodynamic instability or blood loss >500 ml. Red flag (RF_PERIANAL_VENOUS_THROMBOSIS_SEPSIS) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] Severe pain with fever >38 °C, tachycardia, hypotension indicating septic thrombophlebitis.

Perianal venous thrombosis differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Esophageal Varices With Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage and hematemesis rather than an acute painful perianal lump. Compared to Portal Vein Thrombosis: [LLM DRAFT] Typically presents with abdominal pain, ascites, or signs of portal hypertension rather than localized anal symptoms. Compared to Nonpyogenic Thrombosis Of Intracranial Venous System: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with neurological deficits, headache, or seizures rather than a localized thrombosed perianal mass.

Polycythemia neonatorum: A hematology condition known as Polycythemia neonatorum. Common presenting complaints: Polycythemia. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Polycythemia neonatorum red flags. Red flag (RF_THROMBOEMBOLIC_EVENT) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] Stroke, deep vein thrombosis, or renal vein thrombosis resulting from severe hyperviscosity.. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_HEMORRHAGE) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Significant clinical bleeding manifestations such as purpura or gastrointestinal bleeding due to consumptive coagulopathy or hyperviscosity-induced platelet dysfunction..

Polycythemia neonatorum differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Neonatal Jaundice Due To Polycythemia: [LLM DRAFT] Associated elevated bilirubin resulting from the breakdown of excess red blood cells. Compared to Familial Erythrocytosis: [LLM DRAFT] Genetic etiology presenting with persistent erythrocytosis without neonatal environmental risk factors like twin-twin transfusion or placental insufficiency. Compared to Secondary Polycythemia: [LLM DRAFT] Driven by chronic hypoxemia or erythropoietin-secreting processes rather than acute perinatal transfusion phenomena.

Polycythemia vera: In oncology, polycythemia vera (PV) is an uncommon myeloproliferative neoplasm in which the bone marrow makes too many red blood cells. Approximately 98% of PV patients have a JAK2 gene mutation in their blood-forming cells. Common presenting complaints: Polycythemia. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Polycythemia vera red flags. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_ARTERIAL_OR_VENOUS_THROMBOSIS) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] New or worsening stroke, myocardial infarction, deep vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism associated with elevated hematocrit and hyperviscosity.. Red flag (RF_MAJOR_BLEEDING_MANIFESTATION) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Significant gastrointestinal bleeding, severe epistaxis, or abnormal hemorrhage secondary to acquired von Willebrand syndrome or platelet dysfunction..

Polycythemia vera differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Secondary Polycythemia: [LLM DRAFT] Normal or elevated erythropoietin levels due to hypoxia or tumors, unlike the low levels typically seen in polycythemia vera. Compared to Familial Erythrocytosis: [LLM DRAFT] Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with isolated erythrocytosis and normal white blood cell and platelet counts. Compared to Portal Vein Thrombosis: [LLM DRAFT] Can present with splanchnic vein thrombosis secondary to myeloproliferative disorders like polycythemia vera, requiring evaluation of JAK2 mutation status.

Portal vein thrombosis: Portal vein thrombosis (PVT) is a vascular disease of the liver that occurs when a blood clot occurs in the hepatic portal vein, which can lead to increased pressure in the portal vein system and reduced blood supply to the liver. The mortality rate is approximately 1 in 10. Common presenting complaints: Thrombosis. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Portal vein thrombosis red flags. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_VARICEAL_BLEEDING) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Acute massive gastrointestinal hemorrhage due to portal hypertension from portal vein thrombosis, manifesting as hematemesis or melena with hemodynamic instability.. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_MESENTERIC_ISCHEMIA) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] Extension of thrombosis into the mesenteric veins causing severe, disproportionate abdominal pain, peritonitis, and bowel infarction..

Portal vein thrombosis differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Esophageal Varices With Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with acute upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage such as hematemesis or melena, often as a direct complication of portal hypertension. Compared to Chronic Congestive Splenomegaly: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by persistent enlargement of the spleen resulting from long-standing venous outflow obstruction and portal hypertension. Compared to Polycythemia Vera: [LLM DRAFT] A myeloproliferative disorder that serves as a primary hypercoagulable risk factor leading to thrombosis in unusual sites like the portal venous system.

Postmenopausal bleeding: Vaginal bleeding is any expulsion of blood from the vagina. This bleeding may originate from the uterus, vaginal wall, or cervix. Common presenting complaints: Bleeding. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Postmenopausal bleeding red flags. Red flag (RF_HEMORRHAGIC_SHOCK) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Heavy, unremitting postmenopausal bleeding accompanied by hemodynamic instability, dizziness, syncope, or signs of acute blood loss..
Postmenopausal bleeding differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Ovulation Bleeding: [LLM DRAFT] Occurs during reproductive years rather than postmenopause.

Protein deficiency anemia: A hematology condition known as Protein deficiency anemia. Common presenting complaints: Anemia. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Protein deficiency anemia red flags. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_SYMPTOMATIC_ANEMIA) triggered by complaint 'ANEMIA': [LLM DRAFT] Hemoglobin <7 g/dL with tachycardia, hypotension, chest pain or syncope. Red flag (RF_ACUTE_MASSIVE_BLEEDING) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Rapid drop in hemoglobin with signs of hypovolemic shock (tachycardia, hypotension, pallor).

Protein deficiency anemia differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Nutritional Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Broad category requiring dietary history to differentiate specific macronutrient or micronutrient deficiencies. Compared to Scorbutic Anemia: [LLM DRAFT] Associated with vitamin C deficiency and characteristic signs such as petechiae, gingivitis, and perifollicular hemorrhage rather than pure protein malnutrition. Compared to Aplastic Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with pancytopenia resulting from bone marrow failure rather than nutritional inadequacy.

Refractory anemia, unspecified: Anemia is a blood disorder in which the blood has a reduced ability to carry oxygen. This can be due to a lower than normal number of red blood cells, a reduction in the amount of hemoglobin available for oxygen transport, or abnormalities in hemoglobin that impair its function. Common presenting complaints: Anemia. Associated symptoms: Feeling Tired, Pale Skin, Weakness, Shortness Of Breath, Feeling Faint. Risk factors: Blood Loss, Decreased Red Blood Cell Production, Increased Red Blood Cell Breakdown. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Refractory anemia, unspecified red flags. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_THROMBOCYTOPENIC_HEMORRHAGE) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Active, uncontrolled bleeding (e.g., epistaxis, GI bleed, or menorrhagia) resulting from profound bone marrow failure and severe thrombocytopenia.. Red flag (RF_FEBRILE_NEUTROPENIA) triggered by complaint 'RECURRENT_INFECTIONS': [LLM DRAFT] High fever associated with severe neutropenia, indicating a high risk of overwhelming, life-threatening sepsis..

Refractory anemia, unspecified differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Aplastic Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with pancytopenia and a markedly hypocellular bone marrow rather than isolated anemia with dysplastic features. Compared to Fanconi Anemia: [LLM DRAFT] An inherited bone marrow failure syndrome typically presenting in childhood with associated congenital physical anomalies and chromosomal breakage. Compared to Nutritional Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Responds to specific vitamin or mineral supplementation, unlike refractory anemia which persists despite standard therapy.

Scorbutic anemia: A hematology condition known as Scorbutic anemia. Common presenting complaints: Anemia. Associated symptoms: Weakness, Feeling Tired, Changes To Hair, Sore Arms And Legs, Gum Disease, Easy Bleeding. Risk factors: Lack Of Vitamin C. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Scorbutic anemia red flags. Red flag (RF_SEVERE_HEMORRHAGE) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Massive spontaneous hemorrhage, petechial hemorrhages leading to hemodynamic instability, or deep tissue bleeding due to severe vascular fragility from profound vitamin C deficiency..

Scorbutic anemia differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Nutritional Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Broad category lacking the specific cutaneous and skeletal stigmata of vitamin C deficiency such as perifollicular hemorrhages and gum pathology. Compared to Protein Deficiency Anemia: [LLM DRAFT] Associated with generalized malnutrition, edema, and kwashiorkor features rather than the specific hemorrhagic diathesis of scurvy. Compared to Aplastic Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by pancytopenia with bone marrow hypocellularity without the dietary history or connective tissue defects typical of ascorbic acid deficiency.

Secondary polycythemia: Polycythemia is a medical condition suggested by a laboratory finding that the hematocrit and/or hemoglobin concentration are increased in the blood, although this finding is also present in capillary leak syndrome. Polycythemia is sometimes called erythrocytosis, and there is significant overlap in the two findings, but the terms are not the same: polycythemia describes any increase in hematocrit and/or hemoglobin, while erythrocytosis describes an increase specifically in the number of red blood cells in the blood. Common presenting complaints: Polycythemia. Associated symptoms: none listed. Risk factors: none listed. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Secondary polycythemia red flags. Red flag (RF_THROMBOSIS_EMERGENCY) triggered by complaint 'THROMBOSIS': [LLM DRAFT] Acute arterial or venous thrombosis such as stroke, myocardial infarction, deep vein thrombosis, or pulmonary embolism resulting from hyperviscosity.. Red flag (RF_BLEEDING_EMERGENCY) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Severe or uncontrollable hemorrhage, such as major gastrointestinal bleeding, due to acquired von Willebrand syndrome or abnormal hemostasis..

Secondary polycythemia differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Polycythemia Vera: [LLM DRAFT] Associated with JAK2 mutation, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, and low serum erythropoietin levels. Compared to Familial Erythrocytosis: [LLM DRAFT] Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with normal oxygen affinity and high erythropoietin independent of hypoxia. Compared to Polycythemia Neonatorum: [LLM DRAFT] Occurs exclusively in newborns, often due to delayed cord clamping or twin-twin transfusion.

Tuberculous peripheral lymphadenopathy: A hematology condition known as Tuberculous peripheral lymphadenopathy. Common presenting complaints: Lymphadenopathy. Associated symptoms: Fever, Hard, Fixed, Rapidly Growing Nodes, Indicating A Possible Cancer Or Lymphoma, Night Sweats, Runny Nose, Sore Throat. Risk factors: Infections, Autoimmune Diseases, Malignancies, Histiocytoses, Storage Diseases, Benign Hyperplasia, Drug Reactions. Age relevance: . Sex relevance: . Acute or chronic: .

Tuberculous peripheral lymphadenopathy red flags. Red flag (RF_SUPPURATIVE_LYMPHADENITIS_ABSCESS) triggered by complaint 'LYMPHADENOPATHY': [LLM DRAFT] Rapidly enlarging, painful node with overlying erythema, warmth, fever, or systemic signs of infection. Red flag (RF_RUPTURED_NODE_BLEEDING) triggered by complaint 'BLEEDING': [LLM DRAFT] Active bleeding from lymph node or draining sinus, especially with hemodynamic instability.

Tuberculous peripheral lymphadenopathy differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Presents with generalized fatigue and pallor rather than localized lymph node enlargement. Compared to Nutritional Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Characterized by dietary deficiency signs and generalized weakness instead of localized peripheral lymphadenopathy. Compared to Aplastic Anemia Unspecified: [LLM DRAFT] Features pancytopenia leading to bleeding and infections without characteristic regional lymph node enlargement.
